summary: Selene helps students and the public explore a practical question about landing on the Moon: when can a place see the Sun, Earth, or both? Users choose two locations, an arrival date and a stay of 1–12 days, then compare their available time side by side. A shared timeline updates both skies. The catalog includes three south-polar reference regions, all six Apollo landing sites and custom coordinates. An interactive Moon map adds geographic context, while detailed tools reveal angles, intervals and sources. NASA/JPL supplies the position data. Selene compares visibility above a reference horizon, not landing safety, electrical power or guaranteed communication.
details:
A lunar lander using solar panels needs sunlight. Direct communication with Earth also needs Earth above the horizon. These opportunities change with the location and date. Selene makes those differences easier to understand and compare.

The app begins with an animated explanation of sunlight, Earth visibility and why both matter together. In Compare places, users select two locations, an arrival date, a stay of 1–12 days and a priority: sunlight, Earth visibility or both.

Two illustrated cards show the same moment at both locations. Availability bars show when each condition is met. The Side-by-side data view aligns both locations’ hours, complete UTC intervals, sky positions, angles, coordinates and sources. Moving the shared timeline updates both places together.

The catalog includes Shackleton rim, de Gerlache rim, Malapert Massif and the landing sites of Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17. A draggable Moon map uses NASA Moon Trek imagery. Users can also add custom coordinates; their results are explicitly labelled approximate spherical projections from NASA/JPL data.

NASA/JPL Horizons supplies hourly Sun and Earth positions. The app estimates horizon-crossing times between readings, calculates visible intervals and finds when both bodies are visible together. Original responses and retrieval information are retained in the source project.

For November 14–21, 2026, the de Gerlache reference provides approximately 89.8 hours with both bodies above the reference horizon, compared with 75.5 hours at Shackleton: about 14.3 additional hours. This compares available time between those two choices, not landing safety.

Selene uses TypeScript, React, Vite and Three.js. It supports English and Spanish and uses bundled data without requiring a live NASA API connection.

This is an educational prototype. It does not model terrain obstruction, eclipses, batteries, solar-panel output, antennas, radio-link performance or landing hazards. Seeing the Sun or Earth does not guarantee power or communication. Future development could add terrain-derived horizons and broader date coverage.

AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with research, application code, NASA data-retrieval scripts, visibility calculations, tests, interface text, SVG illustrations, animation, documentation and presentation materials. The team directed the interface, requested feature changes and reviewed iterations. AI assistance is acknowledged in the app and project metadata. NASA/JPL Horizons supplied the ephemerides, and cited NASA sources supplied regional/Apollo coordinates and Moon imagery; these source datasets and images were not generated by AI. Custom-coordinate results are explicitly labelled approximate spherical projections calculated in code, not independently queried or certified observations. This is an independent educational student project, without NASA endorsement or mission-grade scientific validation.
